author: Galloway, Lee
title: Office Management: Its Principles and Practice
passage: The filing department has been called a systematized memory. The term is correct so far as it goes, but is not broad enough. Its functions may embrace the following lines and perhaps more: 1. Systematic care of records of all sorts of material not in active use. Such material must be kept safely, in orderly arrangement, must be accessible and yet not in the way. The function here is that of a safe deposit. 2. Service in current business, that is, handling and keeping in order material with which the office is working. Such material must be kept safely, in orderly arrangement, must be quickly accessible, and must be distributed through the office as needed — for instance, at the beginning of each day. Here the function is that of an internal postal system. 3. Collecting, arranging, analyzing of reference material. This may include information compiled by the statistical force in various departments on cards or otherwise. It may include clippings and suggestion memoranda; reports, articles, books, etc. This material must be kept safely, must be sufficiently analyzed and catalogued, and be reasonably accessible. Here the function is that of a library.
context: Galloway's three-function taxonomy maps almost exactly onto the three databases in the information-systems project — the safe deposit function corresponds to the bulk trademark and patent stores, the internal postal function to the candidate and confirmed pipeline, and the library function to the reference literature held here. The taxonomy was in wide circulation by 1918, which means the Kardex and SOUNDEX product lines were being sold into organizations that already understood their records problems in these terms.

author: Galloway, Lee
title: Office Management: Its Principles and Practice
section: Card Index Filing and its neglect
passage: While advancement in filing papers — vertical filing — has been very marked in recent years, the development of card index filing has not been so rapid. This is surprising in view of the fact that the average business house actually needs and should use a great quantity of card index equipment. The reason for the neglect is probably that the average manager does not know the possibilities of card indexing. The word filing has meant to most managers and department heads only the handling of correspondence or current papers. But if the filing of correspondence, invoices, etc., can be made a productive factor in the organization, the same thing is certainly true of card indexing.
context: This passage captures the commercial opportunity that Remington Rand's predecessors were exploiting: the gap between the organizational need for card index systems and the market's incomplete awareness of that need. The KARDEX visible card system addressed exactly this gap — it made the card index's contents visible at a glance without requiring a separate lookup step. Also directly relevant to monthly-image-review: manufacturers like Chicago Pneumatic, operating in the same administrative culture, would have maintained card indexes for their commercial correspondence including trademark filings.

author: Galloway, Lee
title: Office Management: Its Principles and Practice
section: The cross-reference index as organizational infrastructure
passage: If records are required by one department according to subject and by another department according to name, they must not be filed by either name or subject alone. A standardized, cross-reference index must be adopted that will accommodate the various departments. Technical or departmental names should be abolished if they are not in common use throughout the organization.
context: The phonetic indexing problem that the SOUNDEX patent (US1261167A) addresses is a direct instance of exactly this cross-reference challenge. SOUNDEX encodes names phonetically so that variant spellings file together — the Odell patent solves, for name-based records, the multi-department cross-reference problem Galloway identifies here. The passage locates the SOUNDEX invention in its organizational context: it was not an abstract information-retrieval curiosity but a practical answer to a problem every large filing department faced.

author: Leffingwell, William Henry
title: Scientific Office Management
section: Scientific management applied to office records
passage: For thirty-five years the late Frederick W. Taylor devoted all his genius and all his energy to the development of that type of factory management which came to be known as the Taylor system of scientific management. For more than twenty years he was continuously engaged in applying his methods to various kinds of manufacturing establishments. About ten years ago I began the application to office work of the principles of the Taylor system, including planning, analysis, time and motion study, task and bonus plans, and the like.
context: Leffingwell positions filing and card indexing as part of the same scientific revolution that Taylor applied to factory production. This framing explains why Remington Rand's acquisition of the Rand Kardex Bureau and Library Bureau properties carried strategic weight: in the early 1920s, card index equipment was associated with modern scientific management, not mere office furniture. Owning the leading brand in that category was a position in the management consulting economy as much as in the office supplies market.

author: Leffingwell, William Henry
title: Scientific Office Management
section: Systematic card-record keeping in manufacturing offices
passage: The stockkeeper has a card index to the stock, classified and cross-indexed under the following items: As to form number / As to bin number / As to name / As to department / As to use. This extensive cross-indexing has only to be done once and saves an immense amount of time when a new clerk has to look up stock. As a rule, however, since the bin number is on the balance-of-classified-stores record, this number is quoted on the requisition and saves all references to the index by the storekeeper.
context: The card-index cross-referencing practice described here in a manufacturing stock-room context is the same infrastructure applied to trademark and patent records. Chicago Pneumatic, as a manufacturer with multiple product lines, would have maintained similar card records for its commercial properties — including trademark registrations organized by product line, filing date, and registration status.

author: Leffingwell, William Henry
title: Scientific Office Management
section: Vertical filing and the card index decision
passage: There are three ways of filing in a vertical file, viz., alphabetical, numerical and geographical. Each one has its strong points and to each one, of course, some objections can be made. Satisfactory files of each kind are in use throughout the country in various institutions, and necessarily there must be some reason why these files are giving satisfaction. It is of benefit to know the strong points and advantages of each one, in order that after we have examined the conditions in any place, we may be able to decide what kind of arrangement should be presented for a particular kind of business. The alphabetical seems to be the most natural method of filing correspondence.
context: The three-way choice Leffingwell describes is the exact choice that SOUNDEX and VARIADEX were designed to resolve for name-based records. The alphabetical file "seems most natural" but breaks down at scale because of spelling variants — which is the precise problem that phonetic indexing (SOUNDEX) and systematic cross-reference (VARIADEX) addressed.

author: Leffingwell, William Henry
title: Scientific Office Management
passage: It does not require a card index, as the numerical file does, and for this reason is cheaper to install. In the alphabetical file reference is made to the folders direct instead of first to the card in the index and then to the numbered folder, as in the numerical system. All of the correspondence is filed under one system. With the numerical file it is necessary to maintain an alphabetical file for the transient correspondence, as well as those who do not write often enough to warrant giving them a separate folder. So in the numerical file it may be necessary to refer first to the index and then, if no card is found, to the miscellaneous file.
context: This passage documents the overhead cost of card index systems that the KARDEX visible record design was engineered to eliminate. A visible-tab card tray lets the clerk scan the entire index at a glance without a separate lookup step. The engineering problem that produced patents in the information- systems project was, in contemporary management terms, the reduction of motion waste in card-index lookup — which Leffingwell measured and priced in the same way Taylor measured motion waste on factory floors.
